bullets: How to sieve out the primes, add powers when you multiply with the same base, and pack big numbers into standard form
slides.heading: E-Math numbers: primes, indices and standard form
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we sieve for primes, learn when powers add and when they must not, and finish by packing 360000 into standard form.

bullets: Find the primes up to 25 with the sieve and say what makes a number prime
Add the indices when multiplying powers with the same base, and write big numbers in standard form
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: 1 has only one factor - does that make it prime?
25 ends in 5 - can it survive the sieve?
slides.heading: Is 1 a prime? And what about 25?
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands on both questions and take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: the sieve in the first scene settles both.

bullets: A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself
When you multiply powers with the same base, you add the indices
Standard form writes a big number as a value between 1 and 10 times a power of ten
slides.heading: Three tools for numbers
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the map for the whole lesson: primes first, then the index rule for multiplying, then standard form as a way of packaging big numbers.

bullets: Cross out the multiples of 2, 3 and 5 - but keep 2, 3 and 5 themselves
The survivors up to 25 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19 and 23
slides.heading: Primes under the sieve
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: watch the crossing-out mark land on every multiple, and notice that 1 is never in the grid of candidates and 25 falls as a multiple of 5.

bullets: 2^3 is three 2s multiplied and 2^4 is four 2s multiplied
Multiply them and you have seven 2s in a row: 2^3 x 2^4 = 2^7
slides.heading: Same base? Add the powers
slides.notes: Follow the chips as they join the answer slot: three 2s plus four 2s makes seven 2s - counting the factors is why the indices add when you multiply.

bullets: Let the decimal point travel left across 360000 and count the jumps
Five jumps packages it as 3.6 x 10^5
slides.heading: Standard form: big numbers, small package
slides.notes: Watch the point hop left one digit at a time and the power of ten climb with each hop: five jumps, so the power is 5 and the packaged value is 3.6.

bullets: Work each power out first: 2^3 is 8 and 2^4 is 16
Then add the values: 8 + 16 = 24 - the indices stay out of it
slides.heading: Powers do not add when you add
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: the add-the-indices rule belongs to multiplying. When the question adds, work out each power and add the values instead.

bullets: Move the point five places left: 360000 becomes 3.6
So 360000 = 3.6 x 10^5 in standard form
slides.heading: Worked example: packing 360000
slides.notes: Talk through it slowly: the first factor must sit between 1 and 10, and the number of jumps left gives the power of ten.

bullets: List the primes between 20 and 30
Simplify 2^3 x 2^4 and write 45000 in standard form
slides.heading: Your turn: sieve, multiply, package
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them to name the sieving multiples, to count factors for the index rule, and to count the jumps for standard form.

bullets: On your own: one prime question, one indices question, one standard form question
Watch the adding question: work out each power before you add
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the sieve survivors, indices added only when multiplying, and standard form with the first factor between 1 and 10.
